A tort is a civil wrong or an injury, in contrast with a crime. Tort law addresses civil wrongs that harm others regardless of whether any agreement exists between the parties. Tort cases involve harm to people or property and their rights, including property rights, personal rights, and economic interests. A tort claim typically seeks compensation for injury to a person, property, reputation, or economic interest. Tort cases are brought in civil courts, and the remedies are typically monetary damages.
A person who commits a tortious act is called a tortfeasor. A person may be subject to tort liability if they commit a wrongful action, such as defamation, breach of contract, or negligence.
Many jurisdictions allow for the recovery of tort damages in lieu of criminal damages for the same injury. For example, in a civil court, O. J. Simpson was found liable for wrongfully killing his ex-wife and her friend, but acquitted of the criminal charges of murder.

In 2014, Texas Governor Abbott, whose wife suffered complications during her pregnancy, created the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force to examine maternal mortality and morbidity in Texas. The task force’s early analysis found that Black women accounted for about one in nine births in Texas but nearly three in ten maternal deaths. The postpartum period for mothers was also shown to be fraught with potential risks due to lack of access to postpartum care, lack of screening for mental health and other healthcare needs, and inadequate or lack of insurance.
The Task Force’s recommendations covered a wide range of issues from improving antenatal care access and prenatal education, to identifying and treating postpartum depression and improving healthcare team coordination and communication. The Task Force’s findings were shocking and they began to investigate the causes of Texas’s rising maternal mortality rate.
Errors in data
In August 2017, the Task Force reviewed 100 maternal deaths that occurred in Texas over a 12-month period and found that the deaths had been under-reported. Problems with how pregnancy was recorded on death certificates, the way medical examiners and coroners classify and code maternal deaths, and the way data are collected and analyzed led to the underreporting of deaths.
The task force also found that many deaths that were recorded in a hospital setting were unrelated to the pregnancy. These deaths were categorized as indirect obstetric deaths, which occur when pregnancy interferes with or worsens an existing condition, such as a heart problem. However, many of these deaths were later found to be direct obstetric causes, which range from severe bleeding to obstructed labor, for which highly effective interventions exist. The Task Force found that hospital deaths were undercounted because the pregnancy status of a patient was not recorded at the time of death. The task force also reported that many deaths were attributed to obstetric complications but were later found to be related to other causes, such as substance abuse or a preexisting medical condition.
The task force also reported that non-Hispanic black women accounted for 41.74% of maternal deaths in the United States, while making up only 13.8% of the overall population. This gap in maternal mortality is far wider than other countries. However, the discrepancy in the U.S. is not new. According to a study published in the American Association of Maternal and Child Health, black women in the United States have been dying at higher rates than their white counterparts since the 1986-1986 census.
The Task Force’s findings led to a change in how maternal mortality is counted. In 2013, the national US standard death certificate added a “tick box” question on the status of the deceased’s pregnancy. However, many states delayed in adopting the new death certificate standards. This gap led to the task force’s recommendations for more comprehensive data collection and reporting.
The Task Force has since collected data on maternal deaths from all hospitals, long-term care facilities, and maternal death review committees. It also tracks the number of maternal deaths in each county in Texas.
Despite the task force’s efforts, Texas still has the highest maternal mortality rate in the developed world. The task force’s extension is on the special session agenda.
Error reporting
In 2018, the Texas Legislature directed the Department of State Health Services to create the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force to improve data on maternal mortality. The task force’s mission was to identify and investigate any errors in the reporting of maternal deaths in Texas. The task force’s findings led to significant changes in how maternal deaths are reported in Texas.
Despite these changes, however, researchers reported in the Obstetrics & Gynecology that Texas’s maternal mortality rate appeared to roughly double within a few years around 2011. This steep rise was far steeper than in comparable states.
The delay in the postpartum period leaves many health problems unchecked, which can result in maternal death. Women in the US usually meet with their physicians just once after delivery, six weeks after birth, leaving many health problems unchecked.
Errors in data collection
The task force was created to investigate maternal mortality in Texas and to identify any errors in the reporting of maternal deaths. The task force was also tasked with creating a system to track maternal deaths in Texas.
Texas did not expand Medicaid under the PPD. The task force found that the state’s Medicaid program, which covers about half of the state’s births, paid only for the delivery itself, leaving many mothers with limited resources to pay for postpartum care.
The state’s income limits for parents are among the strictest in the country, leaving many women without access to health insurance. Texas is also a right-to-work state, with no minimum wage, which further limits access to prenatal healthcare, which has been shown to increase maternal mortality rates.
The task force found that many doctors are unwilling to see pregnant patients who are uninsured or cannot afford their co-pay, limiting access to prenatal care and awareness of potential complications.
The task force also found that many women report lack of transportation and/or health insurance as reasons they cannot seek prenatal care. And many Medicaid-funded programs do not cover the cost of doula care during the prenatal and postpartum period.
According to a study by Erica L Eliason, cutting Medicaid funding limits access to prenatal healthcare, which has been shown to increase maternal mortality rates. The Task Force recommended that Texas invest in community-based support such as doulas and home visiting programs, which have been shown to potentially improve the health of mother and child and reduce health disparities.

The study of nonverbal communication started in 1872 with Charles Darwin's book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals. For many years, it was believed that facial expressions were not learned expressions or responses, but were instead inherited. The study of body language has grown, and expanded to include body posture and even eye movement. It has been established that up to 93 percent of communication is nonverbal, and that gestures, facial expressions, posture, and gait are all important channels for communication.
The first scientific study of nonverbal communication was published in 1872. Charles Darwin, an acclaimed biologist, wrote The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals. Darwin's research showed that facial expressions of emotion were not specific to culture, and were, in fact, universally understood. He hypothesized that these expressions had evolved in relation to specific emotional states. This was the beginning of the modern study of nonverbal communication. Albert Mehrabian, a pioneer in the study of body language, conducted two experiments in the late 1960's. He measured how people judged feelings and attitudes when someone's words clashed with their tone of voice or facial expression. He found that the disproportionate influence of tone of voice and facial expression became effective only when the situation was ambiguous. Though his work was limited, the figures obtained by combining results from two different studies have been mistakenly assumed to apply to all communication. Mehrabian never claimed that 93 percent of all meaning lives outside language.
Body language is communication using physical behaviors to express or convey information. It is possible to use body language to express emotions, feelings, desires, warning, and states of mind. In the communication process, there are both verbal and nonverbal types of communication. The term body language also refers to several terms which are more accurate in definition and therefore more widely accepted by professionals in the area of body language studies. The study of body language is called kinesics. A person's body language can include their mannerisms, gestures, posture, facial expressions, eye movements, touch, and the use of space. Body language can be used to maintain distance between people while communicating; it can be used to give signals and to send messages. Body language that lacks meaning can create an impasse in a relationship. Body language is a form of nonverbal communication that helps regulate interaction, and can be ambiguous, as two people can easily misinterpret each other's body language. There is no body language grammar system, and one movement can mean many things. Body language must be interpreted broadly, with no absolute meaning for a certain movement. Body language is not culture-specific.
Body language is also a component of nonverbal communication, which involves conscious and unconscious processes of encoding and decoding. In addition to body language, nonverbal communication involves the use of voice and touch, which act as paralanguage. According to modern body language experts, only 7 percent of communication is based on the actual words we say. A useful check is whether your posture reflects the role you want to play in the conversation.

Body language often provides a means of communication that contradicts the spoken message; according to Mehrabian, when verbal and nonverbal communication contradict, the listener will rely on the nonverbal message for interpretation 93 percent of the time. Decoding, also known as interpretation, is the ability to take encoded emotion and interpret its meaning accurately to what the sender intended. As these statistics suggest, body language is critical to effective communication.
The use of body language is subconscious for most people, but those who have a conscious awareness of it can gain a distinct advantage. Body language is perceived subconsciously, and is a critical part of human interaction.

GDP is considered the world's most powerful statistical indicator of national development and progress. GDP per capita figures are important in measuring a country's economic growth (or lack of growth) and in assessing a country's standard of living.
There are limitations with the use of GDP as a measure of a country's economic growth because:
GDP does not take into account income inequality between citizens and the extent of poverty. In a country where the top 1 percent of households earns half of all income, GDP per capita might look healthy, but the typical household would be struggling.
In a country where a small elite controls most of the economy, real GDP per capita might look healthy while the typical household struggles to survive. Factors like class disparity, unemployment and poverty are not included in GDP.
GDP does not include the value of environmental resources and services, which are critical to economic activity. The destruction of natural capital (such as the fish of the sea, the wood of the land) by depletion, degradation, and pollution is not subtracted.
Only production and consumption that are exchanged for money are counted in GDP. For example, the work of housewives and volunteers is not included, nor is the work of black-market dealings. The underground (informal) economy consists of legal goods and services exchanged off the books to avoid taxes or regulation, such as cash-paid babysitting or unreported tips.
GDP includes the value of goods and services produced within the borders of a country, regardless of whether they are consumed within those borders or exported.

GDP is often used as a metric for international comparisons and as a broad measure of economic progress. Sometimes it is viewed as a rival to the Human Development Index (HDI). However, GDP can be a misleading indicator because it is measured in monetary terms. In principle, it can be used to measure the increase in the stock of capital goods and the depreciation of the value of consumer goods, but it fails to account for the overall shift to higher quality of life that may be associated with this change in relative prices.
The GDP per capita in the U.S. was $500, M in 200 500, M in 2015, while in China it was $1,500, M in 200 and $500, M in 2015. A common misconception is that China has achieved higher GDP per capita than the U.S. This is not true because GDP per capita at purchasing power parity (PPP) is used to compare living standards between nations. GDP per capita at PPP is China's GDP per capita of $1,500 multiplied by 4.4 to equal the U.S.'s $500, M.
PPP is the conversion rate for each nation's currency that equalizes the purchasing power of different currencies by using a basket of goods common to each country. PPP largely removes the exchange rate problem but leaves other problems.
PPP takes into account the cost of living (e.g., food, shelter, clothing), but not the quality of living (eants, health care, education). Therefore, the GDP per capita at PPP may be more useful for comparing living standards between nations.
When comparing countries on the basis of welfare economics, the per capita GDP is more informative than the total GDP of each country, as it provides a more accurate reflection of the economic well-being of the inhabitants.
On the other hand, the GDP per capita may not accurately reflect individual living standards. According to economic growth theory, an increase in GDP per capita is often associated with an increase in the standard of living. However, there are problems with using GDP as a measure of economic progress. For example, although GDP is frequently associated with the standard of living, it does not reflect the distinction between economic growth and sustainable development.
GDP is often considered the "world's most powerful statistical indicator of national development and progress," but it has also been criticized as a measure of economic welfare on the basis that GDP consists entirely of economic activity that is measured in money. GDP does not take into account externalities, such as resource extraction, environmental impact and unpaid domestic work. Critics claim it is flawed because it is not wealth, does not measure the overuse of natural resources, provides no distinction between consumer products and investment, includes income that is not useful, and does not count unpaid work.
Critics propose alternative economic models and indicators, such as the OECD's Better Life Index, to measure the effect of the economy on human development and well-being.
GDP per capita is an important indicator of a country's economic performance. It is the ratio of the total gross domestic product (GDP) to the total population, which is also called mean standard of living.
GDP per capita is not a measure of personal income, which makes its use as a standard of living indicator problematic. It is simply a statistic that evaluates the total income earned by individuals in a country during the course of a year, divided by the number of inhabitants. In order to understand how much income is available per person in a country, one must look at real GDP per capita.

In 1999, psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger published findings that people who performed worst on tests of logic, grammar, and humor tended to overestimate their performance the most.
“People tend to have an overly positive self-view. So, if you’re good at something, you tend to think you’re better than you actually are. And if you’re not very good at something, you tend to think you’re not as bad as you actually are.”
- Dunning
Dunning and Kruger explained that the skills needed to do well in a domain are often the same skills needed to judge whether you have done well. When people lack the skills to accurately evaluate themselves, they overestimate their abilities.
The explanation has several implications:
- People who are most in need of help are least likely to accept it.
- The effect may inhibit affected people from addressing their shortcomings to improve.
- The explanation has been used to justify group-based inequalities, which makes it controversial.
The most prominent alternative to the explanation is the statistical explanation, which holds that the effect is mainly a statistical artifact of regression toward the mean combined with the better-than-average effect.
The meta-cognitive explanation holds that poor performers have not yet acquired the ability to distinguish good from bad performances.
Dunning and Kruger’s research indicates that training in a task, such as solving a logic puzzle, increases people’s ability to accurately evaluate how good they are at it.
